A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LoRA hyperparameter optimization framework. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and can be matched despite the changed title, formatting, and table numbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original math-reasoning and code-generation experiments, HPO comparisons, component ablations, and analyses of proxy training and hyperparameter transfer.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds conversation and Bayesmark evaluations, timing measurements, an LLAMBO comparison, and further ablations.

M1.justification: The default algorithm, learned token, projection layer, GP objective, and proxy evaluation remain unchanged. Appendix C introduces an optional automatic prompting procedure: the surrogate learns hyperparameter-performance relationships, and GPT converts those trends into domain-aware prompts. This is a limited procedural extension, evaluated in Table 21.

E1.justification: v2 retains MetaMathQA/GSM8K/MATH and CodeFeedback/HumanEval/MBPP, adds conversation training on WizardLM-Evol-Instruct with MT-Bench evaluation, and extends evaluation beyond LoRA to Bayesmark breast-cancer and Iris classification and diabetes regression. This substantially broadens the represented tasks and domains.

E2.justification: LLAMBO, previously only cited, becomes an evaluated comparator in the LoRA math comparison in Table 18 and the optimization-time comparison in Figure 3. Random search, Optuna/TPE, BO, LBO, and NOMAD remain. The shortened Optuna label does not identify a different baseline.

E3.justification: Appendix B changes Optuna's reported candidates from categorical to integer, and Table 1 corrects the dropout increment from 0.5 to 0.05; these disclosures do not establish that experiments were rerun. Added protocols include MT-Bench GPT scoring, direct GSM8K optimization, alternative embedding models, and timing that excludes proxy training. Bayesmark introduces classification accuracy and negative MSE curves extending to 50 iterations, beyond the retained 30-iteration LoRA setting.

E4.justification: v2 adds PCA-based analysis of embedding geometry, embedding-model sensitivity tests, direct-GSM8K optimization to examine dependence on transfer evaluation, and automatic-versus-manual prompting experiments. These test substantial additional questions about representation, robustness, and reliance on supplied knowledge. The earlier component ablations, proxy correlations, and transfer analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new plots also lack uncertainty bands. LLAMBO's disclosed ten Monte Carlo predictions per iteration describe its internal prediction setting, not uncertainty across experimental runs.

E6.justification: v2 adds conversation, Bayesmark, timing, LLAMBO, embedding-choice, direct-GSM8K, and automatic-prompting results. Most earlier benchmark values remain unchanged. In Table 4, Optuna's GSM8K/MATH scores change from 37.38/4.74 to 54.13/10.50, with its selected configuration also revised in Table 13. These accompany the changed candidate encoding and therefore are replacement results rather than an established same-setting gain.

T1.justification: The GP/deep-kernel formulation, marginal-likelihood objective, and Appendix A gradient derivations are retained. The acquisition symbol changes from alpha to a, and Appendix B adds the standard formula for the already-used Expected Improvement acquisition. These are notation and explanatory additions, without new theoretical reasoning or formal results.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution list retain the same LoRA-specific LLM–BO framework, domain prompting, learned embedding calibration, proxy efficiency, and cross-model applicability claims. The headline claim of over 20% improvement using about 30 iterations remains, and the conclusion is substantively unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands discussion of embedding geometry, optimization-cost tradeoffs, applicability beyond LoRA, operation without manual domain knowledge, and dependence on embedding-model choice. It interprets direct GSM8K results as evidence against transfer alone explaining the gains. It also newly says scale-matched configurations tend to perform best, although unchanged Table 8 frequently favors configurations transferred from the smaller model.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page pointer, conversation hyperparameters in Table 12, and LLAMBO's ten-prediction setting. It revises the Optuna configuration description but omits v1's explicit statement that BO/LBO inputs are five-dimensional. Existing backbone, hardware, training schedule, and prompt-template details are largely retained; the PDFs do not establish what resources the project page actually provides.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for FedPara, WizardLM, MT-Bench, Bayesmark, and Rathore et al. (2025), while dropping the Qwen2.5 technical-report reference. It also explicitly contrasts its GP-based embedding calibration with LLAMBO's prompting approach. The central positioning as LoRA-specialized LLM-assisted BO remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The title changes, wording is polished across the abstract and body, and explanations of the search grid and embedding extraction are clarified. Acknowledgments and an impact statement are added. The basic organization of Sections 1–5 and Appendices A–D remains intact.

P2.justification: The main text and references switch from single-column to two-column conference formatting. v2 adds Figures 2–4, MT-Bench columns, and several appendix tables; merges v1 Tables A3/A4 into Table 13; and moves Table A8 into the main text as Table 9. Figure 1 retains its visualization but gains a clearer caption. These constitute substantial display and layout changes.

improvement.justification: The LLAMBO comparison and embedding/prompt ablations in Tables 18, 19, and 21 address meaningful gaps in v1's validation, while conversation and Bayesmark tests broaden applicability evidence. The net improvement is limited by thin documentation of new evaluation protocols and absent run-level uncertainty. The new scale-matched-best interpretation also conflicts with unchanged Table 8, weakening an otherwise useful expansion of the evidence.
